clinicalPearls: Caused by heterozygous gain-of-function variants in C1R or C1S, subcomponents of the classical complement pathway; autosomal dominant.
The defining feature is severe, early-onset periodontitis beginning in childhood or adolescence and leading to premature loss of teeth.
Lack of attached gingiva and pretibial plaques, which are hyperpigmented atrophic lesions over the shins, are characteristic signs.
Easy bruising and skin fragility are present, while joint hypermobility tends to be limited and often confined to the distal joints.
A positive family history is a core diagnostic criterion, so the pedigree should be traced for early tooth loss and pretibial lesions.
Pretibial plaques often follow minor trauma and appear as brownish discoloured atrophic scars.
Some patients show a marfanoid habitus, acrogeria and prominent subcutaneous vasculature, and vascular events are reported but far less frequent than in vascular EDS.
Distinguish from other causes of aggressive periodontitis and refer for C1R and C1S genetic testing.
reference.pathophysiology: C1R and C1S encode the serine protease subcomponents C1r and C1s of the C1 complex, the first component of the classical complement pathway. The pathogenic variants are gain-of-function or activating changes that promote aberrant autoactivation of the C1 complex, driving inappropriate local complement activation and chronic inflammation. In the periodontium this dysregulated inflammatory response leads to destruction of the supporting connective tissue and alveolar bone, producing the severe early-onset periodontitis and gingival abnormalities, while more generalised connective tissue involvement accounts for the skin fragility, bruising and pretibial plaques. This complement-mediated mechanism is distinct from the collagen and matrix defects that underlie most other EDS subtypes.
additionalDifferentials: Other forms of aggressive or early-onset periodontitis
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive periodontal examination with dental radiographs assessing alveolar bone loss
Molecular genetic testing of C1R and C1S
Skin examination for pretibial plaques and assessment of bruising and fragility
Detailed family pedigree focused on early tooth loss
Echocardiography and vascular imaging if vascular features are present
redFlags: Rapidly progressive periodontitis with tooth loss in a child or young adult
Symptoms or signs of arterial rupture or dissection
Significant unexplained bruising or bleeding tendency
New expanding pretibial or other subcutaneous lesion after minor trauma
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is generally normal, with the major burden being early and progressive tooth loss and its functional and nutritional consequences. Vascular complications are occasionally reported and warrant vigilance where suggestive features exist.
pitfalls: Attributing the severe periodontitis solely to poor oral hygiene and missing the underlying syndrome.
Overlooking a family history of early tooth loss that would support the diagnosis.
Failing to recognise pretibial plaques as a diagnostic clue.
Not offering C1R and C1S genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives.
